opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this was one of the things that really clarified the picture for us. Imagine the model has some fixed probability *p* of getting each individual token right, and that per-token probability improves smoothly and predictably as you scale up the model, which is roughly what you see if you look at cross-entropy loss. Now suppose the task is graded by exact match, so you need to get a whole sequence of, say, *L* tokens all correct to get credit. If you treat those tokens as roughly independent, your probability of success is about *p* to the power *L*.

That simple bit of math does a lot of work. When *p* is moderately below one, *p* to the *L* is essentially zero. As *p* creeps up toward one, *p* to the *L* suddenly shoots up. So you get this sharp, almost step-like curve in accuracy, even though nothing sharp is happening underneath. The model is getting steadily better at every scale; the metric just hides that improvement until the very end. And the longer the answer, the bigger *L*, the sharper and later that apparent jump looks.

What that told us is that a lot of what people were calling "emergence" may be a property of how we measure, not a fundamental change in the model. Nonlinear or discontinuous metrics like exact match or multiple-choice accuracy can turn smooth progress into what looks like a phase transition. When we swapped in continuous metrics, things like token edit distance or the Brier score, on the same model outputs, the curves became smooth and predictable again.

I want to be careful, though. That doesn't mean nothing interesting ever happens with scale, or that exact match is a bad metric. Sometimes you really do care whether the whole answer is right. The point is that if you want to *forecast* capabilities, or claim that something qualitatively new appeared, you have to separate the model's behavior from the lens you're looking through. The fixed-probability model is a nice, almost back-of-the-envelope way to see that the lens alone can produce the effect.

r001.rationale: The response models sequence success as p^L for L roughly independent tokens and explains that as per-token probability improves smoothly, overall exact-match accuracy can jump from near zero to near one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of the argument we made in the paper. The simplest version goes like this. Imagine a model that, for every token it has to predict, gets it right with some fixed probability p. And suppose that p is improving smoothly and predictably with scale, which is exactly what the scaling laws tell us about per-token cross-entropy. There's nothing sharp happening at that level. It's a gentle, well-behaved curve.

Now ask what happens when you measure that same model with accuracy on a task that requires, say, a five-digit arithmetic answer. To get the question right, you have to get all five tokens right. So the probability of success is roughly p to the fifth. And if you plot p to the fifth as a function of scale, it looks very different from p. It stays near zero for a long time and then, right around the point where p gets close to one, it shoots up. That's your emergence curve. It looks like the model suddenly acquired a capability, but underneath, nothing discontinuous happened to the model at all. The discontinuity was manufactured by the metric.

What I find clarifying about the toy model is that it separates two things people tend to conflate. One is the model's actual competence, which is improving smoothly. The other is how a particular measurement compresses that competence into a number. Accuracy is a nonlinear, and in this case multiplicative, transformation of per-token performance. And nonlinear transformations of smooth curves can look as sharp as you like.

And you can check the prediction. If the fixed-probability story is right, then swapping accuracy for a metric that gives partial credit, like token edit distance, should recover a smooth curve. And that's what we saw. Same models, same outputs, different metric, the emergence disappears. Similarly, if you increase the test set size so you can actually resolve small nonzero accuracies, the "flat at zero" region starts to show gradual improvement that was hidden by the resolution of the benchmark.

So I don't want to overclaim. The toy model isn't a full account of everything that happens in these systems. But it's a good null hypothesis. Before you say a capability emerged, you should ask whether a boring model with a smoothly improving per-token success rate, filtered through a harsh metric, would have produced the same picture. Very often, it would.

r001.rationale: The response explains that when each token has success probability p, a task requiring five correct tokens has success probability roughly p⁵, which rises sharply from near zero as p approaches one.

astra-6.text:
One useful way to think about it is to imagine that a model has some fixed probability, p, of getting each step of a task right. If success requires getting all of, say, ten steps right, and we assume those steps are independent, then the probability of success is p to the tenth power.

Now, as you improve the model, p might increase quite smoothly. But when you measure whether the entire task is correct, that smooth improvement can look like a sudden takeoff. For a while, almost nothing succeeds, and then the success rate starts rising quite rapidly.

So this gives us a simple explanation for how an emergence curve can arise without assuming that some fundamentally new capability suddenly switched on. The way we combine individual predictions and score the task can create that appearance. It doesn’t establish that every example of emergence works this way, but it tells us to look carefully at the metric before interpreting a sharp change in accuracy as a sharp change in capability.

r001.rationale: It describes independent task steps each correct with fixed probability p, making all ten correct with probability p^10, and explains that smooth increases in p can yield a rapid rise in measured whole-task success from near zero.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about it is to suppose that a model has some fixed probability, p, of getting each step of a task right. If your evaluation requires it to get all k steps right, then, under an independence assumption, its probability of success is p to the k. So even if that underlying probability improves smoothly as you scale the model, the accuracy on the whole task can look like it suddenly takes off. Below some point, you almost never see a completely correct answer; above it, you start seeing them much more often.

That gives you a simple explanation for at least some emergence curves: the apparent jump can come from how we measure success, without requiring a sudden change in the underlying capability. It doesn’t establish that every instance of emergence works this way, but it means the curve alone isn’t enough to tell us that a new capability appeared abruptly.

r001.rationale: The response explains that requiring all k steps to be correct gives success probability p^k, creating a sudden-looking rise from almost never to more frequent success as p improves. It does not clearly state that overall accuracy can rise to near one.
